packet.evaluation_question: Review respiratory deterioration, hypoxia and abnormal vital signs over serial observations.

evidence.text: If group B streptococcus infection is identified in the woman, trans man or non- binary person within 72 hours after the baby's birth: • ask those directly involved in the baby's care (for example, a parent, carer, or healthcare professional) whether they have any concerns in relation to the clinical indicators listed in box 2 and • identify any other risk factors present and • look for clinical indicators of infection. Use this assessment to decide on clinical management (see recommendation 1.10.3 for the framework for making antibiotic decisions). [2021] Box 2: Clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection (observations and events in the baby), including 'red flags' Red flag clinical indicators: • apnoea (temporary stopping of breathing) • seizures • need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation • need for mechanical ventilation • signs of shock Other clinical indicators: • altered behaviour or responsiveness • altered muscle tone (for example, floppiness) • feeding difficulties (for example, feed refusal) • feed intolerance, including vomiting, excessive gastric aspirates and abdominal distension • abnormal heart rate (bradycardia or tachycardia) • signs of respiratory distress (including grunting, recession, tachypnoea) • hypoxia (for example, central cyanosis or reduced oxygen saturation level) • persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborns • jaundice within 24 hours of birth • signs of neonatal encephalopathy • temperature abnormality (lower than 36°C or higher than 38°C) unexplained by environmental factors • unexplained excessive bleeding, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal coagulation • altered glucose homeostasis (hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia) • metabolic acidosis (base deficit of 10 mmol/litre or greater)
Treat and stabilise any of the following before performing a lumbar puncture: • unprotected airway • respiratory compromise • shock • uncontrolled seizures • bleeding risk. [2024]
Offer parents and carers contact details of organisations that provide parent support, befriending, counselling, information and advocacy. [2012]
Take an immunisation and medicine history, including for drugs that suppress the immune system (such as complement inhibitors). [2024]

claims.text: The infant shows progressive tachypnoea (48 → 60 → 74 breaths/min) and falling SpO₂ (98% → 94% → 90%), which correspond to the NICE‑defined clinical indicators of respiratory distress (E1Q16) and hypoxia (E1Q17), signalling possible early‑onset neonatal infection.
Continue hourly monitoring of respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate and temperature, and document any new red‑flag signs such as apnoea (E1Q7) or need for respiratory support (E1Q9).

Given the deteriorating observations, assess airway and breathing stability before any invasive procedure; if respiratory compromise is present, stabilise the infant (e.g., supplemental oxygen, CPAP) prior to lumbar puncture as recommended (E2Q1‑E2Q3).

Obtain blood cultures, full blood count and CRP, and consider a lumbar puncture once the airway is secured, following the guideline that infection risk assessment should guide antibiotic decisions (E1Q5).
Inform parents of the observed deterioration, the need for further investigations, and provide contact details for parental support services (E3Q1).

claims.text: The infant shows progressive tachypnoea (48 → 60 → 74 breaths/min) and falling SpO₂ (98% → 94% → 90%), which correspond to the NICE‑defined clinical indicators of signs of respiratory distress (E1Q16) and hypoxia (E1Q17), signalling possible early‑onset neonatal infection.
Continue hourly monitoring of respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate and temperature, and document any new red‑flag signs such as apnoea (E1Q7) or need for mechanical ventilation (E1Q9).

Given the deteriorating observations, assess airway and breathing stability before any invasive procedure; if respiratory compromise is present, stabilise the infant (e.g., supplemental oxygen, CPAP) prior to lumbar puncture as recommended (E2Q1–E2Q3).

Investigations should be guided by the clinical risk assessment framework; consider obtaining samples and performing tests that align with identified clinical indicators and the need to confirm infection (E1Q5, E1Q6).
Inform parents of the observed deterioration, the need for further investigations, and provide contact details for parental support services (E3Q1).

packet.evaluation_question: Review respiratory deterioration, hypoxia and abnormal vital signs over serial observations.

evidence.text: If group B streptococcus infection is identified in the woman, trans man or non- binary person within 72 hours after the baby's birth: • ask those directly involved in the baby's care (for example, a parent, carer, or healthcare professional) whether they have any concerns in relation to the clinical indicators listed in box 2 and • identify any other risk factors present and • look for clinical indicators of infection. Use this assessment to decide on clinical management (see recommendation 1.10.3 for the framework for making antibiotic decisions). [2021] Box 2: Clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection (observations and events in the baby), including 'red flags' Red flag clinical indicators: • apnoea (temporary stopping of breathing) • seizures • need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation • need for mechanical ventilation • signs of shock Other clinical indicators: • altered behaviour or responsiveness • altered muscle tone (for example, floppiness) • feeding difficulties (for example, feed refusal) • feed intolerance, including vomiting, excessive gastric aspirates and abdominal distension • abnormal heart rate (bradycardia or tachycardia) • signs of respiratory distress (including grunting, recession, tachypnoea) • hypoxia (for example, central cyanosis or reduced oxygen saturation level) • persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborns • jaundice within 24 hours of birth • signs of neonatal encephalopathy • temperature abnormality (lower than 36°C or higher than 38°C) unexplained by environmental factors • unexplained excessive bleeding, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal coagulation • altered glucose homeostasis (hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia) • metabolic acidosis (base deficit of 10 mmol/litre or greater)
Treat and stabilise any of the following before performing a lumbar puncture: • unprotected airway • respiratory compromise • shock • uncontrolled seizures • bleeding risk. [2024]
Offer parents and carers contact details of organisations that provide parent support, befriending, counselling, information and advocacy. [2012]
Take an immunisation and medicine history, including for drugs that suppress the immune system (such as complement inhibitors). [2024]
